nameStory: The orange anemone gets its straightforward common name from its typically vibrant orange coloration that makes it stand out against rocky surfaces. The scientific name 'Diadumene cincta' comes from Greek roots, with 'diadema' meaning crown or band, referring to the ring of tentacles that crowns this little sea creature like a delicate orange tiara.
description: The orange anemone is a small, delicate sea anemone that looks like a tiny underwater flower with its crown of flowing tentacles. This charming marine animal typically grows to about 1.4 inches tall with a base less than half an inch wide, though some individuals can reach twice that size. Its smooth, slender column supports up to 200 long, graceful tentacles that wave gently in the current. Despite being called the orange anemone, its coloration can vary, though orange tones are most common.

idTips.label: Orange coloration
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive orange hues that give this anemone its name, ranging from bright tangerine to softer peachy tones

idTips.label: Smooth column
idTips.description: The body feels smooth and slippery to the touch, lacking the bumps, ridges, or sticky particles found on many other anemone species

idTips.label: Numerous tentacles
idTips.description: Count up to 200 long, slender tentacles that feel soft and slightly sticky when gently touched, creating a dense crown around the mouth

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically reaches only about 1.4 inches in height with a narrow base, making it one of the more petite anemones you'll encounter

idTips.label: Delicate build
idTips.description: The entire animal has a fragile, graceful appearance with thin tentacles and a slender body that seems almost translucent in good light

habitat: Orange anemones are found in the rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal areas along New England's coast, particularly in the northeastern regions. They prefer to attach to hard surfaces like rocks, pier pilings, and shells in areas with good water circulation. Look for them in tide pools or shallow waters where they can anchor securely while their tentacles catch passing food particles.

seasonality.spring: Orange anemones become more active as water temperatures rise, with tentacles fully extended for feeding during calm weather and incoming tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when anemones are most likely to be spotted with tentacles fully deployed, especially during low tide explorations of rocky shores.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin retracting more frequently as storms increase, though calm days still offer good viewing opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Often contracted into tight, rounded shapes during harsh weather, but can still be found tucked into protected crevices and tide pools.

funFact: Orange anemones can actually clone themselves by splitting in half lengthwise, creating two identical twins from one individual - like having a built-in copy machine that ensures survival even if part of the animal gets damaged by waves or predators!
confusionNotes: Orange anemones are most easily confused with other small Diadumene species, but the orange coloration is usually distinctive. Remember: 'Orange for orange anemone' - if it's bright orange and small with lots of tentacles, you've likely found your match.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the lesser-known anemones in New England waters, with very few recorded observations in the region. Marine biologists are still learning about its distribution patterns along our coast, making any sighting potentially valuable for scientific understanding.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives, the striped green sea anemone has distinctive green coloration with stripes, while the ghost anemone appears much paler or translucent. The orange anemone's vibrant orange coloring and smooth column make it the most colorful of the three Diadumene species, though all share the characteristic delicate build and numerous long tentacles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The striped green sea anemone is easily distinguished from its relatives by its distinctive vertical stripes - the ghost anemone (Diadumene leucolena) is typically white or pale without prominent stripes.
The Ghost Anemone differs from its relative the Striped Green Sea Anemone by lacking the distinctive green coloration and striped pattern of its cousin.
